entry.title: Turning one photo into a 15-second vertical rap video: notes on a template-first AI video pipeline
entry.summary: We run JME Freestyle AI, a small tool that takes a single uploaded photo and returns a 15-second vertical rap video. The interesting part is not the model - it is that we ask the user to choose a template instead of writing a prompt. Prompt-based video generation pushes the failure mode onto the least prepared person in the loop. If someone has never written a shot list, "cinematic dolly-in, 35mm, moody lighting" is a coin flip. A template encodes the shot list once, and the user only supplies what they actually have: one photo. Each template fixes three things: the music style and tempo, so the cut points are known in advance the camera choreography (push in, whip pan, static), so the motion is plausible for the source image the on-screen text structure, so the lyrics land on beats rather…

entry.title: Can you show your auditor every refund your AI agent issued?
entry.summary:
--- https://actaseal.com/notes/ai-agent-refunds-audit-trail.html
Short answer: your books must keep a trail of every refund, and your auditor reports on that trail. The trail shows that a refund was booked. It does not show why your AI agent decided to pay it. Yes, if you keep your books in accounting software. From FY 2023-24, the proviso to Rule 3(1), Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014 requires software that records an audit trail of each transaction, keeps an edit log with dates, and cannot be switched off. A booked refund is one of those transactions. The statutory auditor. Rule 11(g), Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014 makes them state whether the audit trail ran all year, was tampered with, and was preserved. No. When an AI support agent decides a refund inside a support or order tool, the books only show the entry. The reason, the policy rule applied and who approved it stay in that tool, if they are kept at all. Export last month's refunds (order, amount, approver, policy rule, payment reference) and run: import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("refunds.csv") needed = ["order_id", "amount", "approved_by", "policy_rule", "payment_ref"]
missing = df[df[needed].isna().any(axis=1)] print(f"{len(missing)} of {len(df)} refunds can't be traced from decision to payment") print(missing[needed].isna().sum().sort_values(ascending=False))
If approved_by or policy_rule is empty for refunds your AI agent issued, your auditor will see a booked refund with no decision behind it. Question for anyone running an AI agent on refunds: the last time a customer or auditor disputed a refund the agent paid, what record did you actually pull up? A reading of the rules, not legal advice. Sources: ICAI Journal on audit trail requirements (cajournal.icai.org); Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020, Rule 4(10).

entry.title: Agents can pay now. Who checks the agent?
entry.summary: On November 13 OpenAI launched ChatGPT Wallet, built with American Express, Mastercard and Visa. OpenAI's agents can now check out for a user: the agent never sees the card number, it gets a payment token, and the user approves each purchase (US Pro users first; pre-approved spending limits are planned). It joins the card networks' own agent programs (Mastercard Agent Pay, Visa Intelligent Commerce) and x402, which lets any HTTP endpoint charge an agent per call in stablecoins. All of them answer one question well: can this agent pay? Tokens, approvals and limits make sure money moves only when the user allows it. Some go a step further and answer who is this agent?: Visa's Trusted Agent Protocol, for example, lets a merchant recognise a registered agent. None of them answers a third quest…

entry.title: A Million v7 GUIDs and Half Were Still Out of Order
entry.summary: I moved a table's primary key off random GUIDs a little while back. The reason is the usual one: a clustered index hates random inserts. Every new row wants a spot in the middle of the index instead of the end, pages split, the thing fragments, and your inserts get slower the bigger the table gets. Version 7 GUIDs are the tidy fix. They carry a millisecond timestamp in their leading bytes, so new keys sort roughly in creation order and land near the end where the index wants them. Before I trusted that in production I wanted to see the ordering with my own eyes. So I did the dumbest thing that would show it: generate a pile of keys and count how many came out in order. The answer made me feel a bit silly. A v7 GUID isn't random all the way down. The first 48 bits are a Unix millisecond tim…
